title: Carbon — Allotropes and Carbon Monoxide
topicTitle: Carbon: allotropes of carbon (crystalline and amorphous) including fullerenes; properties and uses of carbon monoxide
notes: **Crystalline allotropes — Diamond:** Each carbon atom is sp³ hybridised, forming four equivalent C–C σ bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement with bond angle 109.5°. This 3D network gives diamond the highest known natural hardness (10 on Mohs scale) and a high refractive index of 2.42, responsible for its brilliance. Diamond is an electrical insulator because all valence electrons are locked in strong σ bonds with no free charge carriers.

**Crystalline allotropes — Graphite:** Each carbon atom is sp² hybridised, forming three σ bonds in a planar hexagonal arrangement with bond angle 120°. The remaining p orbital on each carbon overlaps laterally to form a delocalised π electron system across each layer. These weak van der Waals forces between layers (interlayer spacing 3.35 Å) allow layers to slide over one another, making graphite soft and an excellent dry lubricant. The delocalised electrons make graphite a good electrical conductor along the planes.

**Graphene — the 2D wonder material:** A single atomic layer of graphite is called graphene. It exhibits exceptional mechanical strength (tensile strength ~130 GPa, about 200× stronger than steel by weight), extraordinary electron mobility (~200,000 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹), and high thermal conductivity (~5000 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹). Graphene's discovery (2004, Geim & Novoselov, Nobel Prize 2010) opened an entirely new field of 2D materials research.

**Fullerenes — structure and discovery:** Fullerenes are discrete molecular allotropes of carbon consisting of closed cages of hexagons and pentagons. C₆₀ (buckminsterfullerene) has 60 carbon atoms arranged in 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons — exactly the geometry of a truncated icosahedron (football shape). Each carbon is approximately sp² hybridised with some curvature-induced sp².⁵ character. Discovered in 1985 by Kroto, Smalley and Curl (Nobel Prize 1996). C₇₀ has a rugby-ball shape. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with remarkable mechanical and electronic properties.

**Amorphous allotropes — Charcoal and activated charcoal:** Charcoal is produced by heating wood or other organic matter in the absence of air (destructive distillation). Activated charcoal is treated at high temperature with steam or CO₂ to develop an extensive network of microscopic pores, giving it an enormous surface area (~500–1500 m²/g). This makes it an exceptional adsorbent for gases, impurities, and toxins — used in water purifiers, gas masks, and medical treatment of poisoning.

**Amorphous allotropes — Coke and lamp black:** Coke is obtained by heating coal strongly in the absence of air (coking at ~985°C). It contains ~90–95% carbon with small amounts of impurities (S, P, ash). Coke is the primary fuel and reducing agent in blast furnaces for iron extraction. Lamp black (soot) is produced by burning oils or hydrocarbons with limited air supply. It consists of nearly pure amorphous carbon particles and is used as a pigment in inks, printer's ink, and as a reinforcing filler in rubber tyres.

**Allotropes vs. polymorphs — conceptual clarity:** Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state. Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon. Polymorphs refer to different crystal structures of the same compound. Diamond is thermodynamically less stable than graphite at STP (ΔG_f°(diamond) = 2.9 kJ/mol), but the conversion rate is negligibly slow because of the enormous activation energy required to break the 3D covalent network.

**Carbon monoxide — preparation and structure:** CO is produced by incomplete combustion of carbonaceous fuels: $2C + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO$. Industrially, it is obtained by passing steam over red-hot coke (water-gas reaction): $C + H_2O \rightarrow CO + H_2$. Its structure is best described by three resonance forms: $:\text{C} \equiv \text{O}: \leftrightarrow \text{C}^{+} \equiv \text{O}^{-} \leftrightarrow \text{C} = \text{O}$. The C≡O bond length (112.8 pm) is shorter than a typical C=O double bond, reflecting significant triple-bond character. The bond dissociation energy is 1072 kJ/mol, one of the strongest known.

**Carbon monoxide — reducing action in metallurgy:** CO is a powerful reducing agent, especially at high temperatures. In the blast furnace, it reduces iron ore: $Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2$ (zone of reduction, 900–1200 K). It also reduces ZnO ($ZnO + CO \rightarrow Zn + CO_2$) and NiO ($NiO + 3CO \rightarrow Ni(CO)_4 \rightarrow Ni + 4CO$ in the Mond process). The driving force is the high stability of CO₂ (ΔG_f° = −394 kJ/mol) compared to CO at elevated temperatures (Ellingham diagram analysis).

**Carbon monoxide — reactions with metals (carbonyl formation):** CO acts as a ligand forming metal carbonyls through synergic bonding: σ-donation from C lone pair to empty metal d orbitals, and π-back-donation from filled metal d orbitals to CO π* antibonding orbitals. Examples: $Ni + 4CO \xrightarrow{330\,\text{K}} Ni(CO)_4$ (volatile, used in Mond process purification); $Fe(CO)_5$ (iron pentacarbonyl, trigonal bipyramidal); $Cr(CO)_6$ (chromium hexacarbonyl, octahedral). These obey the 18-electron rule.

**Carbon monoxide — reaction with chlorine:** CO reacts with Cl₂ in the presence of activated charcoal catalyst at ~80°C to form phosgene: $CO + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{C} COCl_2$ (carbonyl chloride). Phosgene is a colourless, highly toxic gas used industrially in polyurethane production (via isocyanates) and as a intermediate in organic synthesis. Its toxicity made it a chemical weapon in WWI.

**Carbon monoxide — reaction with strong bases:** When heated under pressure (350–400 K, 50–100 atm), CO reacts with NaOH to form sodium formate: $CO + NaOH \xrightarrow{\Delta} HCOONa$. At higher temperature (~450 K), it forms sodium oxalate: $2CO + 2NaOH \rightarrow (COONa)_2 + H_2$. These reactions highlight the amphoteric character of CO — it can act as both an acid (accepting OH⁻) and a reducing agent.

**Carbon monoxide — toxicity mechanism:** CO binds to haemoglobin (Hb) at the iron(II) centre of the heme group, forming carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb). The binding affinity of CO for Hb is approximately 210–250 times greater than that of O₂, because CO is a stronger σ-donor and π-acceptor ligand than O₂, stabilising the Fe(II) state. Even at 0.1% CO in air, significant COHb forms, reducing O₂ transport capacity and shifting the O₂ dissociation curve leftward (cooperativity effect), impairing O₂ release to tissues — a doubly dangerous effect.

**Uses of carbon monoxide:** (1) Reducing agent in iron and steel production (blast furnace). (2) Component of synthesis gas (CO + H₂, called water gas or syngas) used to produce methanol ($CO + 2H_2 \rightarrow CH_3OH$), acetic acid (Monsanto process), and hydrocarbons (Fischer–Tropsch synthesis). (3) Phosgene production for polyurethanes. (4) Metal carbonyl synthesis in organometallic chemistry. (5) Historical use as a fuel gas (coal gas contained ~50% CO).

**Safety — CO as the silent killer:** Carbon monoxide is colourless, odourless, and tasteless, making it impossible to detect without instruments. It is produced by any incomplete combustion — faulty furnaces, car exhaust in enclosed spaces, charcoal grills indoors. Symptoms of CO poisoning (headache, dizziness, nausea) are often mistaken for flu. Recommended CO detectors should be installed near sleeping areas. The permissible exposure limit (PEL) is 50 ppm for 8 hours (OSHA). Immediate first aid is fresh air and oxygen therapy (100% O₂ or hyperbaric oxygen).
confusion: ❌ Diamond is a good conductor of electricity because it is a form of carbon. ✅ Diamond is actually an electrical insulator — all four valence electrons of each carbon are locked in strong sp³ σ bonds with no free electrons. Graphite conducts electricity due to delocalised π electrons.

❌ Graphite and diamond have the same density. ✅ Diamond has a density of 3.51 g/cm³ while graphite has 2.25 g/cm³. Diamond's tightly packed 3D covalent network is far denser than graphite's loosely bound layered structure.

❌ CO is an acidic oxide and dissolves in NaOH to form a salt without special conditions. ✅ CO does not react with NaOH at room temperature. It requires heating under pressure (350–400 K, 50–100 atm) to form sodium formate (HCOONa). This is exceptional for a neutral oxide.

❌ CO is more toxic than NO because it has an unpaired electron. ✅ NO actually has an unpaired electron (free radical), while CO is diamagnetic (all electrons paired). CO's toxicity arises from its much higher binding affinity for haemoglobin (~210× that of O₂), not from radical reactivity.

❌ Activated charcoal and charcoal are the same substance. ✅ Regular charcoal has limited surface area. Activated charcoal is specially treated (steam or chemical activation at high temperature) to create a vast network of micropores, increasing surface area to 500–1500 m²/g — making it far superior for adsorption.

❌ C₆₀ (buckminsterfullerene) has all hexagonal rings like graphite. ✅ C₆₀ contains exactly 12 pentagonal rings and 20 hexagonal rings. The 12 pentagons are required (by Euler's theorem) to close the cage into a sphere. Pure hexagonal networks form flat sheets (graphene), not closed cages.

❌ The Mond process purifies nickel by converting it to Ni(CO)₄ at high temperature. ✅ The Mond process works in two temperature stages: Ni reacts with CO at ~330 K to form volatile Ni(CO)₄, which then decomposes at ~450 K to deposit pure nickel and release CO. The low-temperature formation and high-temperature decomposition are both essential.
practice:
**Problem 1:** A sample of activated charcoal adsorbs 0.5 g of CO gas at STP. If the surface area of the charcoal is 800 m²/g, calculate the average area occupied by one CO molecule on the surface. (Molecular mass of CO = 28 g/mol; Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³). 

**Solution:**
Moles of CO = $\frac{0.5}{28} = 1.786 \times 10^{-2}$ mol.
Number of molecules = $1.786 \times 10^{-2} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.075 \times 10^{22}$ molecules.
Total surface area = 800 m².
Area per molecule = $\frac{800}{1.075 \times 10^{22}} = 7.44 \times 10^{-20}$ m² = $74.4$ Å².
**Answer: 74.4 Å² per CO molecule.**

**Problem 2:** In a blast furnace, 100 kg of Fe₂O₃ is reduced by CO. Calculate (a) the mass of Fe produced and (b) the volume of CO required at STP. (Fe = 56, O = 16). 

**Solution:**
Molar mass of Fe₂O₃ = 2(56) + 3(16) = 160 g/mol.
Moles of Fe₂O₃ = $\frac{100 \times 10^3}{160} = 625$ mol.
From $Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2$:
(a) Moles of Fe = 2 × 625 = 1250 mol.
Mass of Fe = $1250 \times 56 = 70{,}000$ g = **70 kg**.
(b) Moles of CO = 3 × 625 = 1875 mol.
Volume of CO at STP = $1875 \times 22.4 = 42{,}000$ L = **42 m³**.

**Problem 3:** Calculate the bond order and predict the magnetic behaviour of CO using molecular orbital theory. (Total electrons = 14). 

**Solution:**
MO electron configuration for CO (14 e⁻): $\sigma_{1s}^2 \; \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \; \sigma_{2s}^2 \; \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \; \pi_{2p}^4 \; \sigma_{2p}^2$.
Bond order = $\frac{N_b - N_a}{2} = \frac{10 - 4}{2} = 3$.
All electrons are paired → **diamagnetic**.
The triple bond (bond order = 3) is consistent with the short bond length (112.8 pm) and high bond dissociation energy (1072 kJ/mol).

**Problem 4:** A gas mixture contains CO and CO₂. When 100 mL of the mixture is exploded with excess O₂, the volume decreases by 20 mL. Calculate the percentage composition of the original mixture. 

**Solution:**
The reaction is: $2CO + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2$.
Volume contraction = volume of O₂ consumed = $\frac{1}{2} \times$ volume of CO.
Given contraction = 20 mL, so volume of CO = $20 \times 2 = 40$ mL.
Volume of CO₂ = $100 - 40 = 60$ mL.
% CO = $\frac{40}{100} \times 100 = 40\%$.
% CO₂ = $\frac{60}{100} \times 100 = 60\%$.
**Answer: 40% CO, 60% CO₂.**

**Problem 5:** In the Mond process, 5.87 g of impure nickel is converted to Ni(CO)₄ and then decomposed to give 2.00 g of pure nickel. Calculate the percentage purity of the original sample. (Ni = 59). 

**Solution:**
Moles of pure Ni obtained = $\frac{2.00}{59} = 0.0339$ mol.
From the process: Ni (impure) → Ni(CO)₄ → Ni (pure), the mole ratio is 1:1.
Mass of pure Ni in sample = 2.00 g.
Percentage purity = $\frac{2.00}{5.87} \times 100 = 34.07\%$.
**Answer: 34.07% pure nickel.**

**Problem 6:** A person breathing air containing 0.05% CO by volume for some time has a certain percentage of carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) formed. If the binding affinity ratio $\frac{K_{CO}}{K_{O_2}} = 210$, and air contains 21% O₂, estimate the ratio [COHb]/[HbO₂] at equilibrium. 

**Solution:**
Using the competitive binding equilibrium: $\frac{[COHb]}{[HbO_2]} = \frac{K_{CO}}{K_{O_2}} \times \frac{[CO]}{[O_2]}$.
Fraction of CO in air = $\frac{0.05}{100} = 5 \times 10^{-4}$.
Fraction of O₂ in air = $\frac{21}{100} = 0.21$.
$\frac{[COHb]}{[HbO_2]} = 210 \times \frac{5 \times 10^{-4}}{0.21} = 210 \times 2.38 \times 10^{-3} = 0.500$.
This means [COHb] ≈ [HbO₂] — half the haemoglobin is carrying CO instead of O₂!
**Answer: The ratio is approximately 0.5 (50%), indicating severe CO poisoning.**
universalFacts: Diamonds are not forever — at room temperature and pressure, diamond is thermodynamically unstable relative to graphite (ΔG = −2.9 kJ/mol). However, the kinetic barrier to conversion is so enormous that a diamond will persist essentially forever at ambient conditions. Only at temperatures above ~1500°C in inert atmosphere does diamond begin converting to graphite at an appreciable rate.

Fullerenes were discovered almost by accident: in 1985, Harold Kroto, Robert Curl, and Richard Smalley were studying carbon chains in red giant stars using a laser vaporisation technique. They unexpectedly found C₆₀ and C₇₀ clusters, won the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and opened the field of nanocarbon science.

Carbon monoxide is naturally produced in the human body: haem oxygenase enzymes break down haem (from ageing red blood cells) to produce biliverdin, iron, and CO. Endogenous CO acts as a signalling molecule in vasodilation and anti-inflammatory pathways — the same molecule that is deadly as a pollutant is a vital biological messenger.

Graphene's thermal conductivity (~5000 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) exceeds that of diamond (~2000 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) and is about 10× that of copper. Its electrical conductivity and electron mobility are similarly extraordinary, making it a candidate for next-generation electronics, flexible displays, and ultra-fast sensors.

The CO in cigarette smoke binds to haemoglobin with ~210× the affinity of O₂. A heavy smoker (20 cigarettes/day) can have 5–10% of their haemoglobin converted to COHb, equivalent to breathing air at 1500–2000 m altitude. This chronic mild asphyxiation contributes to cardiovascular disease and reduced exercise tolerance in smokers.
